opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So the basic idea behind concept erasure is pretty simple to state: you want to take some representation inside a neural network, say the activations at a particular layer or the embeddings, and remove the information about a specific concept from it, while changing the representation as little as possible otherwise. The concept might be something like gender, or race, or part of speech, or really any attribute you can label in your data.

The way I like to make "remove the information" precise is in terms of what a classifier can do. In our work on LEACE, which stands for LEAst-squares Concept Erasure, we focused on linear erasure. The goal is that after you've edited the representation, no linear classifier can predict the concept any better than a trivial constant predictor that just guesses the base rate. It turns out there's a nice characterization of when that's true: linear guardedness holds exactly when the class-conditional means of the representation are all equal, or equivalently when the cross-covariance between the representation and the concept label is zero. Once you have that condition, you can ask for the edit that achieves it while moving the data as little as possible, in a least-squares sense, and that has a closed-form solution. That's what LEACE gives you.

Why care? I see a few motivations. One is fairness: if you don't want a downstream model relying on, say, gender, you can try to make that information inaccessible. But I'm actually more excited about the interpretability and science side. Concept erasure works as a causal intervention. If you surgically remove a concept from a network's internals and measure how its behavior changes, you learn whether and how the network was using that concept. We did this with part-of-speech information in language models, erasing it at every layer and watching performance degrade, which tells you the model really depends on that kind of syntactic information.

I should be upfront about the limits. Linear erasure is exactly that, linear. A sufficiently expressive nonlinear probe might still recover the concept, and information can be encoded in ways that aren't captured by the means. So it's not a guarantee that the information is gone in an information-theoretic sense. But because so much of what neural networks seem to do is surprisingly linear, at least in how downstream layers read from upstream ones, linear erasure gets you a lot of mileage, and it has the huge advantage of being cheap, provably optimal for what it promises, and easy to reason about.

r001.rationale: The response says concept erasure removes information about a specific concept from a neural network representation.

r002.rationale: It says to change the representation as little as possible otherwise and describes the edit as minimizing movement in a least-squares sense.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about concept erasure is: you have some representation, say the activations of a neural network, or even just the input features, and you want to remove all the information about some particular concept, like gender or part of speech, while leaving everything else as intact as possible. So you want to surgically delete one thing and preserve the rest of the content.

The motivation is twofold. One is fairness. If you're worried that a downstream model is going to use a protected attribute, you can scrub that attribute from the features it sees, and then by construction it can't rely on it, at least not in the way you've erased it. The other, which is the one I personally find more interesting, is interpretability. If you erase a concept from a model's representations and then observe how its behavior changes, that gives you a causal handle on what that concept was actually being used for. That's much stronger evidence than just training a probe and seeing that the information is present, because information being decodable doesn't tell you the model uses it.

The tricky part is defining "all the information." Early methods would train a linear classifier, project out its direction, and repeat, but you can always find another probe, so it never really converges. With LEACE, what we did was ask a cleaner question: what is the smallest change to the representation that makes it impossible for any linear classifier to do better than chance at predicting the concept? It turns out there's a closed-form answer. You need to make the class-conditional means all equal, and you want to do that with the minimum mean-squared-error perturbation. That gives you a provable guarantee against linear adversaries, and it's cheap enough to apply at every layer of a transformer.

Of course, linear erasure doesn't stop a nonlinear probe from recovering the concept, and we're pretty upfront about that. But a lot of the evidence suggests networks make heavy use of linearly represented features, so removing the linearly available information often has a real effect on behavior. And having a well-defined, optimal solution to a precisely stated problem feels like a better foundation than heuristics that you hope are good enough.

r001.rationale: It says concept erasure removes information about a particular concept from a representation, including neural network activations.

r002.rationale: It says to leave everything else in the representation as intact as possible, which covers unrelated information.

astra-6.text:
The goal of concept erasure is to remove information about a particular concept from a model’s representations while preserving as much other information as possible. Suppose you have a representation of a person’s occupation, and it also encodes their gender. You might want to erase the gender information while retaining the information relevant to the occupation.

But you have to specify what it means for information to be removed. If a linear classifier can no longer predict gender from the representation, that’s a particular guarantee; it doesn’t necessarily mean a nonlinear classifier couldn’t recover it. So the goal needs to be defined relative to a class of predictors.

It’s also useful as an experimental intervention. You erase information and see how the model’s behavior changes, which can help you investigate whether that information was playing a role in a task.

r001.rationale: It says concept erasure removes information about a particular concept from a model’s representations; the context identifies this as deep learning.

r002.rationale: It says to preserve other information and gives the example of retaining occupation information while erasing gender information.

sol-6.1.text:
The goal of concept erasure is to take a representation inside a neural network and remove the information about some particular concept, while preserving as much of the other information as possible. So, for example, you might want to remove information about gender from a representation without destroying its usefulness for the task you care about.

The tricky part is defining what it means for that information to be gone. If a linear classifier can no longer predict gender, that tells you it’s inaccessible to linear classifiers; it doesn’t necessarily mean a nonlinear classifier couldn’t recover it. So you need to specify the class of predictors you’re trying to guard against.

And there’s a scientific motivation too: you can erase a concept and see how the model’s behavior changes. That gives you a way to investigate whether the model actually uses that information, rather than merely whether you can decode it from its activations.

r001.rationale: The response says concept erasure removes information about a particular concept from a representation inside a neural network.

r002.rationale: It says the goal is to preserve as much other information as possible while removing the target concept.
